episodes.180812: A moist and convective environment produced thunderstorms with gusty winds across central Nevada.
episodes.180893: A squall line developed to the northwest of Tennessee early on July 18, 2023, and quickly traveled southeast through the early afternoon and evening hours. Damaging winds were the primary threat with this squall line with wind gusts of 60 to 70 mph common. Numerous reports of downed trees and power lines were received before the squall line finally weakened as made its way into eastern Middle Tennessee.
episodes.180901: Numerous to widespread strong and severe thunderstorms developed during the late afternoon amid a favorable environment of up to 3000 J/kg of CAPE and 30 knots of deep shear, while lift was initiated by an upper wave and associated low-level boundary across northern central Indiana.  Scattered large hail was focused over the western and northern portions of the Indianapolis Metro and near Bloomington.  Several storms produced damaging winds near the Interstate 69 corridor, and eventually in southeastern central Indiana as the episode continued into the evening.  Greatest damage ranged from several trees downed in both southeastern Hamilton County and Jackson County to damaged orchard crops amid several reports of up to 2.00 inch hail in Hendricks County.
episodes.180903: After high pressure dominated eastern Utah for several days, moisture gradually increased ahead of an approaching system. This led to the development of isolated to scattered high-based thunderstorms. Given the dry air at the lower levels, gusty outflow winds were the primary threat from storms. The stronger storms produced gusty winds in excess of 58 mph across Grand County.
episodes.180986: A squall line developed over southeast Missouri and moved rapidly east-southeast across western Kentucky and extreme southern Illinois. Areas along and south of a line from East Cape Girardeau to Golconda received widespread strong winds. Isolated damaging winds occurred. The bow-shaped squall line formed from a cluster of thunderstorms over central Missouri during the late morning hours. South of a surface front that extended from central Missouri to the I-64 corridor of southern Illinois, rapid heating of a moist air mass produced strong instability. A core of strong mid-level winds from 50 to 60 knots in the vicinity of the storms aided in rapid propagation and organization of the storms.
episodes.180992: A squall line developed over southeast Missouri and moved rapidly east-southeast into western Kentucky. Locally damaging winds occurred shortly before the squall line exited Missouri. The bow-shaped squall line formed from a cluster of thunderstorms over central Missouri during the late morning hours. South of a surface front that extended from central Missouri to the I-64 corridor of southern Illinois, rapid heating of a moist air mass produced strong instability. A core of strong mid-level winds from 50 to 60 knots in the vicinity of the storms aided in rapid propagation and organization of the storms.
episodes.180999: A squall line developed over southeast Missouri and moved rapidly east-southeast across western Kentucky. Areas along and southwest of a line from Hopkinsville to Princeton to Smithland received widespread strong winds. Locally damaging winds occurred, especially from Ballard County southeast across the Paducah, Mayfield, and Kentucky Lake regions to Hopkinsville. The bow-shaped squall line formed from a cluster of thunderstorms over central Missouri during the late morning hours. South of a surface front that extended from central Missouri to the I-64 corridor of southern Illinois, rapid heating of a moist air mass produced strong instability. Mixed layer cape values climbed above 3000 j/kg. A core of strong mid-level winds from 50 to 60 knots in the vicinity of the storms aided in rapid propagation and organization of the storms across western Kentucky.
episodes.181019: Thunderstorms brought locally heavy rain to Monmouth County on the afternoon of July 18.  Rainfall totals were as high as 1.5 to 2.5 inches.
episodes.181211: Preexisting hot and muggy conditions contributed to unsettled weather in West Virginia on both July 17th and 18th. Each afternoon observed strong to severe thunderstorms sprouting during peak heating hours, with damaging winds and a few instances of hails accompanying convection. Tree damage was the primary result of the passing storms, especially across portions of central and southern West Virginia.
episodes.181261: Unsettled weather festered over southeast Ohio on July 17th and 18th in the midst of hot and muggy conditions. On the 17th, two rounds of thunderstorms swept through the area, leading to downed trees across Athens, Meigs, and Lawrence Counties.||On the next day, an upper level disturbance provided additional support for strong to severe thunderstorms. In the span of an hour, downed trees occurred from strong winds across Lawrence, Vinton, and Meigs Counties. A strong downburst took place in Meigs County, leading to approximately 70 knot winds in several areas. This resulted in primarily tree damage in the eastern half of the county over into parts of West Virginia.
episodes.181268: A passing upper level disturbance with additional contribution from preceding hot and muggy conditions led to strong to severe thunderstorms on the afternoon of July 18th. In the span of around 45 minutes, damaging wind gusts swept through Greenup County and led to numerous areas of downed trees. The quick pace of storms allowed activity to quiet down quickly in eastern Kentucky as convection pressed eastward.
episodes.181383: Scattered showers and thunderstorms west of the Laramie Range on the afternoon of the 17th resulted in strong downburst winds, especially over Carbon County near Interstate 80 and the North Snowy Range Foothills.
episodes.181384: Storms developed over the Nebraska Panhandle late in the afternoon on the 18th including a discrete severe thunderstorm over Cheyenne County, Nebraska with quarter size hail resulting in crop damage.
episodes.181385: A thunderstorm moving offshore produced a strong wind gust in Fort Pierce.
episodes.181401: A line of thunderstorms with damaging wind gusts moved through Scranton and surrounding areas. Multiple trees were knocked down across the area.
episodes.181432: A small complex of thunderstorms organized over the Mississippi River Valley before moving southeast into western Kentucky. Strong winds accompanied the leading edge of the storms. The storms occurred ahead of a cold front that trailed southwest from the Great Lakes across central Missouri.
episodes.181433: Isolated strong to severe thunderstorms over the Ozark foothills gradually organized into a small complex of thunderstorms as they moved east into the Mississippi Valley. Sporadic damaging wind gusts and large hail accompanied the strongest storms. The storms occurred ahead of a cold front that trailed southwest from the Great Lakes across central Missouri.
episodes.181434: A small complex of thunderstorms tracked eastward across western Kentucky during the early evening hours. Sporadic tree damage and large hail accompanied the strongest storms, most of which followed a west-to-east corridor through Paducah to Princeton. The storm occurred ahead of a cold front that trailed southwest from the Great Lakes across central Missouri.
episodes.181558: A cold front swept through Central New York and kicked off scattered showers and thunderstorms. There was enough instability to support isolated severe thunderstorms. There were a few reports of trees knocked down by the strong winds.
episodes.181603: A weak cold front produced isolated thunderstorms along the south shore of Lake Ontario anchored along the lake breeze. Though the storms did not last more than a few hours, they produced scattered wind damage as they tracked along the south shore of Lake Ontario.
episodes.181604: There were severe storms that rode along the south shore of Lake Ontario.
episodes.181654: Clusters of slow-moving, training, and heavy rain producing thunderstorms resulted in a downed tree and flash flooding over parts of eastern New York on July 18. The bulk of the heaviest rain and flooding reports were concentrated in and around the Capital District including the City of Albany, where some cars were stuck in rising flood waters. More than 5,000 residents in Albany County lost power as a result of these storms.
episodes.182015: Typical summer afternoon convection formed.  There were many heavy showers and thunderstorms with gusts to 30-45 mph (non-severe).  Lightning from one storm caused a power pole fire in Hatfield, MA.
episodes.182129: Two rounds of scattered thunderstorms occurred on July 17th as a cold front moved through central Illinois. The first round of thunderstorms occurred during the early afternoon, and then additional development occurred during the evening. Both rounds of thunderstorms produced large hail, primarily near or just south of the I-72 corridor.
episodes.182146: A supercell thunderstorm developed over central portions of Campbell County and tracked southeast across northern parts of Weston County. The storm produced large hail and gusty winds, causing some damage along its path.
episodes.182147: A long-lived supercell thunderstorm tracked from northeastern Wyoming across southwestern South Dakota, producing very large hail and wind gusts over 60 mph across portions of Custer, Fall River, and Oglala Lakota Counties.
episodes.182155: An early morning severe thunderstorm developed over portions of Todd County, producing hail to golf ball size.
episodes.182156: A supercell thunderstorm developed southeast of the Black Hills and tracked across western and southern portions of Oglala Lakota County before moving into Nebraska.
episodes.182174: While impactful storms remained outside (to the north) of the forecast area, robust supercell storms developed across south-central Kansas during the afternoon of the 17th. Given a very hot and well-mixed boundary layer, heat burst events occurred beneath the anvil of these storms across portions of Alfalfa County. This included a severe-caliber wind gust near the community of Cherokee.
episodes.182253: Scattered showers and thunderstorms with heavy rainfall developed of the Western Maine Mountains on the afternoon of the 18th. Moist air supported torrential rainfall rates between 2 to 3 inches an hour, all of which fell over saturated soils. Localized flash flooding resulted where storms trained over the same locations.  A localized outflow wind gusts associated with one of the flash flood thunderstorms also downed some trees.
episodes.182254: Scattered showers and thunderstorms with heavy rainfall developed across the White Mountains and areas northward on the afternoon of the 18th. Moist air supported torrential rainfall rates between 2 to 3 inches an hour, all of which fell over saturated soils. Localized flash flooding resulted where storms trained over the same locations.
episodes.182273: West to northwest upper winds were across south central and central Nebraska. Most unstable CAPE and deep layer shear were fairly high across the area. A shortwave disturbance resulted in thunderstorm development the previous afternoon across the High Plains. Those thunderstorms moved southeast and impacted south central and central Nebraska during the early morning hours of July 18th. These thunderstorms were moving along an instability axis and produced a 60 mph wind gust in Adams County at 2:17 AM CDT. The storms moved through the rest of the area without any more severe reports. Another complex of storms moved into the area and produced quarter sized hail in Valley County just before 7 AM CDT.
episodes.182340: Thunderstorms developed during the afternoon and evening hours ahead of a cold front moving through the Ohio Valley.
episodes.182341: Thunderstorms developed during the afternoon and evening hours ahead of a cold front moving through the Ohio Valley.
episodes.182342: Thunderstorms developed during the afternoon and evening hours ahead of a cold front moving through the Ohio Valley.
episodes.182344: Scattered thunderstorms developed along a boundary that had stalled across the the Ohio Valley.
episodes.182518: Scattered thunderstorms, some with torrential rainfall affected scattered areas across Vermont on July 14. Two to locally four inches of rain fell in a some areas, leading to a few reports of flash flooding and road washouts.
episodes.182644: An upper level storm system moved into Virginia late in the evening and with enough instability in place, a few scattered storms developed. One of the storms became severe, producing pockets of damaging winds across the New River Valley.
episodes.182920: Thunderstorms developed along a cold front brought severe weather to central South Dakota during the evening hours. A storm moved into Pierre and Fort Pierre, SD, producing hail. There were numerous reports of baseball-sized hail across the area, and even one larger than a softball, with an estimated diameter of 5.0 inches. The hailstone is the largest on record in Hughes County (4.0 in Pierre on 6/30/1997 and Blunt on 8/26/2018). Damage was done to vehicles, roofs, and other outside structures. The storm also produced a brief tornado about 11 miles south of Fort Pierre, just west of US Highway 83, around 6:45 pm CDT. These storms then moved south and east through the evening, producing large hail and damaging winds. A wind gust of 100 mph was recorded just west of Oacoma at 8:15 pm CDT via a weather station from the South Dakota State University's mesonet. Damage was done to power poles, trees, trailers, and other property in and around Oacoma.
episodes.182926: A squall line dropped south-southeast from middle Tennessee through north Alabama during the mid to late afternoon hours of the 18th. One brief tornado was spawned along the line in northern Madison County, and numerous other reports of wind damage were received.
episodes.183069: Thunderstorms initiated across portions of southeast AZ during the afternoon hours. With high pressure centered over the Arizona/New Mexico border, the steering flow was from the southeast so as a result storms were steered northwestward into portions south-central AZ, including portions of Pinal County and southern Maricopa County. The storms weakened approaching the Greater Phoenix area due to strong convective inhibition. With moderate instability with MLCAPE ranging between 500-1000 J/KG and DCAPE in excess of 2,000 J/KG, conditions were favorable for strong downburst winds and outflows, which resulted in areas of dense blowing dust across portions of Pinal and Maricopa Counties.
episodes.183237: A modest push of monsoon moisture and ongoing extreme heat fueled spotty thunderstorms over southern Nevada. Isolated high winds and flash flooding occurred.
episodes.183273: A slow moving trough moved through the American Samoa Islands from July 12 through July 18th. WSO Pago Pago recorded 3.68 inches of rain during that time.
episodes.183312: A series of short waves moved across there region and interacted with the very hot and moist air mass that had been in place. Thunderstorms moved front the northwest to the southeast across the region and several became severe.
episodes.183329: Thunderstorms developed during the afternoon and moved northwest across southeast Arizona through the evening. Storms produced damaging winds and large hail across eastern Pima County and the Tohono O'odham Nation and a dust storm in Pinal County. The Catalina Foothills were especially hit hard with numerous power poles downed leaving thousands without power for two days.
episodes.183346: Perhaps the most impactful severe weather in July spread from northwest into central and southeast sections of the state on the 14th/15th. Two to more than three inches of rain fell from Fort Smith (Sebastian County) to Waldron (Scott County) and Mena (Polk County). ||Little Rock National Airport (Pulaski County) had a gust of 58 mph. A tree fell on a camping vehicle at Diamond City (Boone County), and a barn was overturned near Whiteville (Baxter County). Trees were toppled near Fairview (Ouachita County).||There were spotty instances of hail/damaging wind across the northern and central counties on the 17th/18th.
episodes.183367: Thunderstorms developed during the afternoon of the 18th. An isolated severe thunderstorm produced damaging winds near the town of Guerette in northeast Aroostook county. Several trees were toppled around Cross Lake. One tree fell on a house...with another tree toppled on to power lines.
episodes.183415: A warm, muggy and unstable air mass was in place across eastern Kentucky on July 18th as a wavering front remained northwest of the Lower Ohio River. The first storm cluster of the day fired over central Kentucky during the early afternoon hours before moving into eastern Kentucky. This initial round of storms impacted areas primarily north of the Hal Rogers Parkway during the late afternoon and early evening. The combination of dry air in the mid-levels and sufficient shear led to a a couple of strong bowing line segments with estimated peak wind gusts in the 60 to 70 mph range. The most numerous instances of wind damage, primarily downed trees and power lines, were observed in Estill, Lee, Montgomery and Bath counties. A gust of 61 mph was recorded at the RAWS site close to the Jackson National Weather Service Office. A second larger convective system dropped into the the Commonwealth during the mid-afternoon but then decayed as it moved onto the Cumberland Plateau. However, some cells with this system will still strong enough to bring a few instances of severe wind damage to portions of southcentral Kentucky.
episodes.183462: Thunderstorm clusters, including some supercells, moved southeast across portions of north central Nebraska during the early morning hours of July 18. Some hail was significantly severe, measuring over 2 inches.
episodes.183463: An isolated supercell initially moved south through the panhandle during the mid and late afternoon hours of July 18, which was responsible for very large hail and some damaging winds. Additional storms developed ahead of that cell toward the Colorado border. A second round of storms, including clusters and a supercell, moved through north central Nebraska shortly after and produced very large hail.
episodes.183479: A shift in the atmospheric pattern from mid to late July brought an array of impacts to much of Utah, including severe thunderstorm wind gusts, large hail, and flash flooding.
episodes.183534: Storms occurred from the early afternoon to the evening of the 17th ahead of the southward moving cold front. The storms mainly affected locations along and east of a line from Stockton to Springfield to Branson, and produced hail up to 3 inches in diameter at Preston in Hickory County. Wind damage and wind gusts over 70 mph were also reported. The town of Theodosia in Ozark County was especially hard hit with widespread tree damage. Rainfall accumulations averaged between one to two inches, with isolated accumulations over three inches in Laclede and Camden counties.
episodes.183722: Large hail and damaging winds were reported across western Kansas.
episodes.183864: Hot and unstable southwest winds led to the formation of thunderstorms across parts of SE Florida as the Atlantic seabreeze moved inland.
episodes.183925: On the afternoon of July 17th, a supercell developed near Grandview and moved to the southeast through Raymore, Harrisonville, Garden City, and continued on into WFO Springfield's area. This supercell produced very large hail, including a 5 hail stone near Garden City.
episodes.183976: Scattered thunderstorms developed over the North Carolina mountains during the afternoon. A couple of these storms produced brief damaging wind gusts. A weakening line of thunderstorms then moved into the mountains from east Tennessee late in the evening. These storms produced additional isolated damaging wind gusts.
episodes.183979: An isolated storm developed over the Blue Ridge mountains and moved southeast into upstate South Carolina during the evening. The storm produced brief damaging wind gusts over northern Pickens County. A cluster of storms later moved into the Upstate from western North Carolina during the early morning hours and produced additional isolated damaging wind gusts.
episodes.184009: Multiple mesoscale convective systems developed in northwest flow aloft and tracked across the Mid-South. The first tracked from southeast Missouri and southwest Kentucky into West Tennessee during the early-mid afternoon on July 18th. The second mesoscale convective system developed over southern Missouri and tracked across northeast Arkansas, the Memphis metropolitan area, and north Mississippi. These systems were supported by a very moist and unstable airmass with surface-based convective available potential energy values exceeding 6000 J/kg and precipitable water values greater than 2 inches. Adequate amounts of wind shear aloft helped to organize storms as well. Numerous severe storms occurred across the Mid-South with a few reports of large hail and many reports of damaging wind. The Memphis area was among the hardest hit with power outages to over 130,000 utility customers in Shelby County.

episodes.184080: Drier air aloft was in place during the afternoon, and only a few cells were able to form. The dominant one that formed used that dry air to produce damaging gusty winds over southeast Louisiana.
episodes.184106: A weak cold front moved across a marginally unstable air mass across central-southern VT during the afternoon and evening hours of July 18th. A few thunderstorms developed with one storm producing localized wind damage.
episodes.184115: A lingering upper level trough lingered over the northeast CONUS. At the surface, a slow moving cold front moved through western NY and western PA, while a pre-frontal trough developed ahead of it. The pre-frontal trough became the focus for convection and a broken line of severe thunderstorms moved over the waters.
episodes.184169: A very strong area of high pressure that brought record heat to northern Arizona in the previous few days started to move eastward. This allowed a southerly flow to develop over the area transporting moisture northward from Mexico. This moisture allowed for the development of scattered showers and thunderstorms over parts of northern Arizona.
episodes.184185: A strong thunderstorm formed over Michigan's eastern upper peninsula during the late morning and moved southeast over Lake Huron, producing a waterspout that was observed near Mackinac Island.
episodes.184289: Persistent southerly flow brought a very moist airmass into the region ahead of a slow moving upper level disturbance and slow moving surface frontal boundary during the afternoon of July 18th.  Storms developed by early afternoon brining isolated areas of wind damage and large hail to both Southern and Northern New Hampshire.
episodes.184400: Another active period of weather set up across central Kentucky and southern Indiana July 17th and 18th, 2023 as multiple waves of showers and thunderstorms moved across the region, bringing damaging straight-line winds, severe hail, and one tornado to the region. The synoptic pattern was fairly consistent (albeit active) during this period, with large-scale mid- and upper-level troughing extending from Hudson Bay down into the Ohio Valley. In the low-levels, a quasi-stationary front extended from the mid-Mississippi Valley across central Indiana and into northern Ohio, with a seasonably warm and unstable air mass present across the Ohio Valley, which was primarily located south of the low-level frontal boundary. The first wave of strong to severe storms developed during the late afternoon hours in the vicinity of the frontal boundary across central Indiana. As these cells morphed into a quasi-linear convective system during the evening hours, the combined cold pool development forced the storms southward into southern Indiana and central Kentucky. Ahead of the line of storms, mixed-layer CAPE on the order of 1500-2500 J/kg and effective bulk shear of 30-40 kt provided a favorable parameter space to sustain strong-to-severe convection. This line of storms ultimately produced sporadic wind damage and near-severe hail across southern Indiana and north central Kentucky, with convection lingering into south central Kentucky overnight before gradually dissipating in the early morning hours on July 18th.||While sporadic convection continued through the morning hours on July 18th, the next main wave of strong and occasionally severe thunderstorms arrived during the early afternoon hours. With unseasonably fast flow continuing aloft, wind shear remained sufficient for multicell clusters and a few supercells to develop across central Kentucky. Instability remained moderate to high, with low-to-mid 70s dewpoints and temperatures in the 80s allowing for the development of 2000-3000 J/kg MLCAPE. This initial wave of cells produced scattered wind damage and hail mainly across the Kentucky Bluegrass. Additionally, a decaying mesoscale convective system coming in from western Kentucky also produced scattered wind damage across southern and central Kentucky. One brief spin-up tornado developed within this line over Marion County, producing EF0 damage. Convection dissipated once the line of storms cleared the area around sunset. As a result of multiple waves of heavy rainfall moving over the same areas, scattered occurrences of flooding were observed across the area, with the most concentrated area of flooding occurring over eastern Jefferson County and Shelby County, Kentucky.

Multiple rounds of strong to severe thunderstorms moved through the Marion County area during the afternoon and evening hours on July 18th. A very|brief tornado touched down about 4 miles east of Lebanon, KY near|U.S. 68 just before 7 pm EDT. The storm was moving to the|northeast at 40 mph. There were several trees twisted and snapped|and an older barn was destroyed. Most of the damage was facing to|the east northeast, with some exceptions.||Some of the roof truss from the barn was lofted northeast, but the|board became impaled and was leaning back toward a southwesterly direction. ||A horse trailer weighing over 1000 pounds was moved off the block|about 3 feet towards the northwest. This was the highest rated |part of the tornado at 80 mph.||A section of a tree was snapped and facing back to a |southeasterly direction. ||The resident of the property showed where the tree line was |behind the barns, and the top of the tree line had about a 20-foot|swath cut out of it.||The top of another metal pole barn exhibited evidence of uplift.||Just beyond the second barn was an uprooted hardwood tree at |the end of the tree line. It was facing north northeast. This was |the last damage observed from both ground and aerial drone survey.
